# Open research {#open-research .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Section 3
:::

::: notes
The vocabulary tells us what each kind of check is, and open research concerns whether anybody can carry one out. A reproduction needs your data and your code, a robustness check needs your data, and running the study again needs your materials. This short section goes through the practices one at a time, asking of each what it lets another person do with your work, and then you apply them to a paper that you know well.
:::

## Open research: the practices {#open-research-the-practices .smaller}

::: {.small}
| Practice | What it makes possible |
|---|---|
| **Open data** | Someone else can re-analyse your evidence |
| **Open code** | Someone else can rerun your exact analysis |
| **Open materials** | Someone else can run your study again |
| **Open access** | Someone else can read the claim in the first place |
| **Preregistration** | A dated record of the analysis plan, filed in a registry before the results exist |
| **Registered reports** | Peer review of the plan, with publication decided before results |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Each one removes a specific obstacle, and none of them guards against every problem. The programme, set out at length: [@MunafoEtAl2017ManifestoReproducibleScience]
:::

::: notes
Each of those reviewers needed something from you before they could start, your code, your data or your materials, and open research is a set of practices that supply such things, each removing a specific obstacle. Open data let someone else reanalyse your evidence, open code lets them rerun your exact analysis, and open materials let them run the study again in a new sample. Open access lets them read the paper at all, which sounds trivial until you try to obtain a paper from outside a wealthy university. A preregistration is a dated record of the analysis plan, filed in a registry before the results exist, and a registered report goes further, since the plan is peer-reviewed and the decision to publish is taken before any result exists. [advance] None of these practices guards against every problem, and Munafò and colleagues set out the whole programme at length.
:::

## Discussion – a paper you know {#discussion-a-paper-you-know .questionslide}

::: {.none .nonincremental}
Take a published quantitative paper that you know well, one of your own or one from your reading.

- Which of the six practices did it follow?
- To reproduce its main result, what would you need first, and where would you get stuck?
- Which of the three Rs could a reader test with what its authors made public?
:::

::: notes
Now a short discussion, in pairs. Take a quantitative paper that you know well, one of your own or one that you have read closely, and put the six practices to it. Then the harder question: if you set out tomorrow to reproduce its main result, what would you need first, and where would you get stuck? If the first step, the data, stops you, you are in good company, because the next session shows that most attempts at reproduction stopped there when somebody measured it on six hundred papers. [state the time] I will then ask two or three of you which of the three Rs a reader could test from what the authors released, and what was missing for the other two.
:::
